newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Oct 14.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Oct 14.

text.p: Labour was guardedly optimistic New Zealand First leader Winston Peters would come through as queen-maker, giving New Zealand its first female prime minister in Helen Clark. Certainly, the earliest signs for Labour were good - Mike Moore was talking to NZ First adviser Michael Laws yesterday about preliminary negotiations. However, senior National figures made it clear they would not give away government easily, and intented to make an attempt to find common ground with Peters. Page 1.

The government will carry on today with Prime Minister Jim Bolger at the head of a caretaker administration until the next government emerges. Governor-General Sir Michael Hardie Boys issued a written statment reiterating he would not be taking a hands-on role in coalition agreements. Cabinet is due to meet this morning. Page 1.

Brierley Investments chief executive Paul Collins has a salary package of $1.437 million a year, making him the highest-paid businessman in New Zealand indentified so far. Collins heads a list of four BIL executives paid more that $1 million each. Page 1.

Maori voters made an astonishing electoral turnaround on Saturday, forsaking an almost unblemished 60-year marriage to Labour in favour of NZ First. Winston Peter's party swept the five Maori seats, winning four overwhemingly. Page 2.

NZ First's caucus is likely to prefer a coalition with Labour to one with National. The influence of leader Winston Peters will be crucial, but among the party's 17 new MPs, at least 10 can be expected to lean toward Labour. Though they have been directed not to comment on coalition prospects, some have declared or indicated their inclinations in the past. Page 3.

National's first post-election caucus meeting on Tuesday is expected to include a fingerpointing session on what went wrong with the party's campaign. National had sets as its target 40 percent of the party vote, but ended up just above 34 percent. Page 3.

Financial markets may face short-term uncertainty in the currency and bond markets, analysts say, but any movements are likely to be small. Markets won't be surprised by the election results because they were in line with poll predictions. ANZ bank chief economist Paul Stewart said markets were likely to react cautiously or even a little nervously "but the impact won't be too dramatic". Page 21.

New Zealand's election result was largely in line with Standard and Poor's expectations, and the ratings agency was broadly comfortqble with it, S&P sovereign risk managing director David Beers said. Page 21.

The sharemarket is expected to go into limbo after Saturday's election failed to clarify anything from last week, according to brokers. Though the market could experience some volatility in the next two or three weeks as the power brokers sort out their differences, there was no reason to suggest a change in investment strategy, they said. Page 21.

Top-level contact has already begun between Labour and New Zealand First to prepare for post election negotiations. A telephone call from Labour's Mike Moore to the New Zealand First strategist Michael Laws was the first discussion between the parties after Saturday's historic MMP election which left Winston Peters holding the balance of power. National Party strategists are brainstorming ways the New Zealand First could be accommodated in a centre-right coalition or persuaded to support a minority National government. Page 1. --

The international credit ratings agency Standard and Poor soothed concerns about financial market reaction to Saturday's election saying it was comfortable with the outcome. The agency's sovereign risk director David Beers said a change of government, if any, would not necessarily mean a change from existing economic policy. Page 1.

Prime Minister Jim Bolger failed to lift National's vote to the needed 40 percent, but his job as party leader will not come under immediate threat. National MPs approached on Sunday were unanimous there was no need to do anything precipitate and Bolger would probably survive until at least the middle of next year.
United's sole remaining MP Peter Dunne is likely to formally take over party leadership this week.

ACT NZ leader Richard Prebble claims the election night result is a victory for the centre-right. The former Labour cabinet minister said National could continue either as a minority government with support from ACT's eight new MPs or with a clearly majority in coalition with New Zealand First.

Up to half of the payment to Brierley Investments' executives was incentive-based, the company said on Sunday as it disclosed that four of those executives earned more than $1 million a year. And, in the past year, shareholders received a gross return of 33 percent through the combination of a 22 percent increase in share price and the payment of 9 cents a share in dividends, a BIL spokesman said.
Little reaction is expected to Saturday's election result when financial markets open on Monday.
